samasa.literal: she whose own form is all
samasa.sense: the Goddess who is everything that exists (cf. 1.82 सदसद्वाखिलात्मिके)
samasa.alt: As a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (सर्वस्य स्वरूपम्, ‘the true nature of all’) the compound would be neuter, with the vocative सर्वस्वरूप; the feminine vocative -e shows the bahuvrīhi.

samasa.sense: possessing every power — the gods’ powers gathered in her (2.10–19, 8.12–21)

morph.note: Imperative second singular with the ending -हि, as in पाहि and याहि: √त्रा is the athematic by-form of the root that also appears as त्रायते, त्रायस्व.
Ablative plural: with verbs of protecting, the danger one is protected from stands in the ablative.
समन्वित is the past participle (kta) of सम् + अनु + √इ (adādi 2P ‘to go’): ‘gone along with’, hence ‘accompanied by, endowed with’, taking the instrumental.

mantras.anvaya: हे सर्वस्वरूपे सर्वेशे सर्वशक्तिसमन्विते देवि, नः भयेभ्यः त्राहि। हे दुर्गे देवि, ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three bahuvrīhi and tatpuruṣa vocatives, then a prayer (त्राहि नः) and a new refrain addressed to Durgā.
mantras.lit: O you whose form is all, O Lady of all, O you endowed with every power — protect us from fears, O Devī; O Durgā, O Devī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: Form of all things, Lady of all, possessed of every power — protect us from every fear, Devī. Durgā, Devī, salutation to you.

comm.t: The refrain changes. After sixteen stanzas ending नारायणि नमोऽस्तु ते (11.8–23), the gods address her as Durgā and ask for protection from fear. From here to 11.28 each stanza is a prayer for protection, as at the end of the gods’ hymn in chapter 4 (4.24–27 शूलेन पाहि नो देवि …).

The name Durgā is explained later in this chapter: the Devī foretells that she will slay the asura Durgama and be known as Durgā Devī (11.49–50). Traditionally this stanza is among the most widely recited of the Saptaśatī, used on its own as a prayer for freedom from fear.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has दुर्गा (name 190), सर्वेश्वरी (name 202), सर्वशक्तिमयी (name 199) and भयापहा (name 121), ‘remover of fear’. Shared names and ideas; the works are separate.

samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (लोचनत्रय)
samasa.literal: adorned with a triad of eyes
samasa.sense: the three-eyed face of the Goddess

morph.note: Imperative third singular of √पा ‘to protect’ (पाति, पातु): the face, not the Goddess, is its subject — the start of a series in which her face, trident, bell and sword are asked to protect.
Not a separate word: भूषित, the past participle (kta) of √भूष् (curādi 10 ‘to adorn’), is the last member of लोचनत्रयभूषितम् and takes the gender of वदनम्.

mantras.anvaya: हे कात्यायनि, एतत् लोचनत्रयभूषितं सौम्यं ते वदनं नः सर्वभीतिभ्यः पातु। ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject (वदनम् with three qualifiers) and the imperative पातु; then the refrain to Kātyāyanī.
mantras.lit: May this gentle face of yours, adorned with three eyes, protect us from all fears; O Kātyāyanī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: May this gentle face of yours, graced with three eyes, protect us from every fear. Kātyāyanī, salutation to you.

comm.t: The first of four stanzas (11.25–28) in which the Goddess’s own attributes — her face, trident, bell and sword — are asked to protect. The gods began this hymn by praising her as Kātyāyanī (11.2 कात्यायनीं तुष्टुवुः), and the asuras sought her under that name (8.29 यत्र कात्यायनी स्थिता).

The gentle face is asked first, the fierce weapons after. The gods of chapter 4 prayed in the same order of thought: ‘protect us with your gentle forms and with your terrible ones’ (4.26 सौम्यानि यानि रूपाणि … यानि चात्यर्थघोराणि तै रक्षास्मान्).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has कात्यायनी (name 556) and त्र्यम्बका (name 762), ‘the three-eyed’. Shared names; separate works.

samasa.type: prādi tatpuruṣa (the prefix अति as first member)
ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa with the agent noun सूदन, containing a karmadhāraya (अशेषासुर); अशेष is itself a nañ bahuvrīhi (न विद्यते शेषः यस्य)
samasa.literal: destroyer of the asuras without remainder
samasa.sense: the trident that slew every asura
the trident, weapon of Māheśvarī (11.14) and of the Devī (4.24)
the dark, fierce Goddess who is kindly to her devotees
samasa.alt: Also read ‘Kālī who brings good (भद्रम्)’; the compound’s form is the same. In a karmadhāraya the feminine first member takes its masculine form (भद्र-, not भद्रा-).

morph.note: Ablative singular of the i-stem भीति ‘fear’ (गुण of the final + -ः); the same form serves as the genitive. Here it is ‘from fear’, with पातु.
सूदन is an agent noun in -अन from √सूद् (‘to destroy’), as in मधुसूदन; neuter here to agree with त्रिशूलम्.

mantras.anvaya: हे भद्रकालि, ज्वालाकरालम् अत्युग्रम् अशेषासुरसूदनं (ते) त्रिशूलं नः भीतेः पातु। ते नमः अस्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is three qualifiers of त्रिशूलम्, the subject of पातु; then the refrain to Bhadrakālī.
mantras.lit: May the trident — dreadful with flames, exceedingly fierce, destroyer of the asuras without remainder — protect us from fear; O Bhadrakālī, let homage be to you.
mantras.tr: May your trident, fearsome with flames, fiercer than fierce, slayer of every asura, protect us from fear. Bhadrakālī, salutation to you.
mantras.tr_note: ‘your’ is supplied from the context of the series (ते in 11.25 and 11.28).

comm.t: The trident is asked to protect. It is Māheśvarī’s weapon (11.14 त्रिशूलचन्द्राहिधरे; 8.49 माहेश्वरी त्रिशूलेन) and the first weapon named in the gods’ prayer of chapter 4 (4.24 शूलेन पाहि नो देवि). The name Bhadrakālī closed the account of the second carita’s hymn (4.39 तथेत्युक्त्वा भद्रकाली बभूवान्तर्हिता नृप).

The name joins two opposites: भद्र, ‘auspicious’, and काली, ‘the dark one’. The weapon that destroyed every asura is the protection of those who take refuge in her; the fierce form is fearsome only to what is hostile.
A modern reading: the prayer is not ‘protect us from enemies’ but ‘protect us from fear’ (भीतेः). The danger named is the inner state as much as the outer threat.

-aḥ before the voiced d becomes -o. The digital text writes देवि and पापेभ्यो together without a space; nothing changes there (i before p).

sandhi.type: visarga sandhi (with an avagraha in print)
sandhi.note: -aḥ before the voiced n becomes -o: पापेभ्यो नः. The text prints an avagraha (पापेभ्योऽनः) as though an a had been elided after the o, but no word अनः fits the sentence, and the metre counts eight syllables either way (the avagraha is silent). It is read as पापेभ्यो नः (see flags).

sandhi.rule: ङमो ह्रस्वादचि ङमुण्नित्यम् (8.3.32) does not apply
sandhi.note: The n is doubled only after a short vowel; after the long ā of सुतान् it simply joins the next vowel.

samasa.sense: the fiery might of the demon hosts

morph.note: √हिंस् is a rudhādi (seventh-class) root: the strong present inserts न before the final consonant, and the root’s own nasal falls away: हि-न-स्-ति (pl. हिंसन्ति).
Absolutive of the prefixed causative-type stem आ-पूरय-: with a prefix the absolutive takes -य (ल्यप्) and the stem’s -अय- is dropped: आपूर्य ‘having filled’.
Neuter s-stem plural: तेजस् → तेजांसि, with lengthened vowel and the nasal before s (as मनांसि, यशांसि).

The enclitic नः occurs twice. The first is the object of पातु (‘protect us’); the second is taken as genitive with पापेभ्यः (‘from our sins’). It may also be the object repeated for emphasis; the sense hardly changes.

mantras.anvaya: हे देवि, या (घण्टा) स्वनेन जगत् आपूर्य दैत्यतेजांसि हिनस्ति, सा घण्टा नः पापेभ्यः नः पातु, सुतान् इव।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या … हिनस्ति, with the absolutive phrase स्वनेन जगत् आपूर्य) describes the bell; the main clause is सा घण्टा … पातु; सुतान् इव is a comparison.
mantras.lit: Which, having filled the world with its sound, destroys the fiery strength of the daityas — may that bell, O Devī, protect us from our sins, as children.
mantras.tr: Your bell, whose sound fills the world and breaks the daityas’ strength — may that bell, Devī, guard us from our sins, as children are guarded.
mantras.tr_note: ‘as children are guarded’ renders सुतान् इव; the Sanskrit does not name who guards them. ‘Your’ is supplied from the series.

comm.t: The bell is asked to protect. In the battle the Devī’s bell swelled the lion’s roar (8.9 घण्टास्वनेन तन्नादमम्बिका चोपबृंहयत्), and in the fight with Śumbha she filled the quarters with its sound, ‘which destroyed the strength of all the daitya armies’ (9.20 निजघण्टास्वनेन … समस्तदैत्यसैन्यानां तेजोवधविधायिना). The stanza recalls that line almost word for word (हिनस्ति दैत्यतेजांसि).

The sound that undid the demons’ strength is now asked to guard against sins: the outer enemy of the narrative becomes the inner enemy of the worshipper. The gods asked the same in chapter 4 (4.24 घण्टास्वनेन नः पाहि). A bell is rung in the rite of worship, and the hymn gives that sound a protective sense.
A modern reading: ‘as children’ makes the protection parental, not military — the same power that terrifies the hostile is tender toward its own.

flags.uncertain: The printed पापेभ्योऽनः carries an avagraha that grammar does not explain; read as पापेभ्यो नः (पापेभ्यः + नः). No word अनः fits here, and the avagraha does not affect the syllable count; it may be a printing habit of the source. The digital text also writes देविपापेभ्यो without a space. The text is kept as printed.

samasa.vigraha: असृक् च वसा च असृग्वसे; असृग्वसयोः पङ्कः असृग्वसापङ्कः; असुराणाम् असृग्वसापङ्कः असुरासृग्वसापङ्कः; तेन चर्चितः
samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas (असुरासृग्वसापङ्क, असृग्वसापङ्क) and an itaretara dvandva (असृग्वसा)
samasa.literal: smeared with the mud of the blood and fat of the asuras
samasa.sense: the sword still wet from the battle
samasa.alt: असृग्वसापङ्क may also be a karmadhāraya of metaphor (असृग्वसे एव पङ्कः, ‘the mire that is blood and fat’); the meaning is the same.
Also a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa, करेण उज्ज्वलः, ‘bright through (being held in) the hand’; the saptamī is simpler.

morph.note: Past participle of √नम् in the active sense (an intransitive root of motion and posture): ‘(we are) bowed’, with the accusative त्वाम् of the one bowed to. The copula अस्मः is understood.
Dative of purpose: ‘for good, to (our) welfare’ — what the sword is to serve.
Imperative third singular of √भू, the thematic present भव- + -तु: ‘may it be’.

mantras.anvaya: हे चण्डिके, असुरासृग्वसापङ्कचर्चितः करोज्ज्वलः ते खड्गः (नः) शुभाय भवतु। वयं त्वां नताः (स्मः)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A benediction (खड्गः … शुभाय भवतु) with two qualifiers of the sword, and a closing statement (वयं त्वां नताः) in place of the refrain.
mantras.lit: Smeared with the mire of the asuras’ blood and fat, gleaming in your hand — may your sword be for (our) good, O Caṇḍikā; we are bowed to you.
mantras.tr: Your sword, flashing in your hand and smeared with the blood and fat of the asuras — may it be for our good, Caṇḍikā. We bow to you.
mantras.tr_note: ‘our’ is supplied: शुभाय names no one.

comm.t: The last of the protection stanzas asks the sword to be ‘for good’. It is the weapon with which the Devī cut down Muṇḍa (7.21) and beheaded Niśumbha (9.33, 9.36), and which the gods named among her weapons in 4.27 (खड्गशूलगदादीनि … तैरस्मान् रक्ष सर्वतः). The refrain becomes a plain statement: ‘we are bowed to you’.

A sword still wet with blood is asked for auspiciousness. The gods of chapter 4 already saw the paradox: her weapons purify even the enemies they strike, who go to the higher worlds (4.18–19 लोकान् प्रयान्तु रिपवोऽपि हि शस्त्रपूता). The violence is directed at what threatens the world.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has चण्डिका (name 755). The name is shared; the works are separate.
